title: Combining Human 3D Neural Models and 96-Well MEA Systems to Accelerate Drug Discovery
body_markdown:
Over the last two decades, advances in stem cell biology and electrophysiology have transformed how researchers study the human brain *in vitro* . Human pluripotent stem cell-derived neural models, including organoids, spheroids, and neural aggregates, have enabled scientists to recreate key aspects of human neuronal development and network function in a laboratory setting.


Unlike traditional two-dimensional cultures, these three-dimensional systems better preserve cellular interactions and provide a more physiologically relevant environment for neuronal maturation. Early studies independently demonstrated that stem cell-derived neurons could form functional neuronal networks and respond to pharmacological modulation, establishing an important foundation for modern neurobiology and drug discovery research \[1-3\].


### From Single-Well MEAs to Scalable Human Neural 3D Models


At the same time,[microelectrode array (MEA) technology](https://www.multichannelsystems.com/) emerged as a powerful tool for measuring network-level electrophysiological activity. Initial experiments combining pluripotent stem cell-derived neural models with MEAs were typically performed using[single-well systems equipped with 60 electrodes](https://www.multichannelsystems.com/products/mea2100-mini-systems) . While these robust platforms enable detailed characterization of neuronal activity and are still used prolifically today, throughput may be limited, making concentration-response studies labor-intensive, costly, and time-consuming.


Today, the introduction of[24-well and 96-well MEA systems](https://www.multichannelsystems.com/products/incub8-multiwell-mea-system) offers the potential to dramatically increase scale and efficiency. But can complex human pluripotent stem cell-derived 3D neural models be successfully translated from single-well systems into a robust and scalable 96-well format?


### Oscillution's Approach to Scalable Neuropharmacology


One company working to answer that question is[Oscillution](https://www.oscillution.com/) , a preclinical services company that supports pharmaceutical and biotechnology organizations in the discovery and development of therapies for neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases. By combining human 3D neural electrophysiology models with advanced multi-electrode recording technology, Oscillution has developed a platform designed to provide more predictive insights into human neuronal function than conventional preclinical assays. Their human 3D neural models are benchmarked against human brain tissue and enable rapid assessment of compound effects on neuronal network activity.


Central to this approach is the[Incub8™ Multiwell MEA System](https://www.multichannelsystems.com/products/incub8-multiwell-mea-system) from Multi Channel Systems, which provides several advantages for modern drug discovery programs:


- **High-throughput multiwell screening capabilities** that enable scalable testing across large experimental datasets.
- **Advanced analysis software** for evaluating spiking activity, network bursting, local field potentials, and other electrophysiological parameters.
- **Modular scalability** that allows researchers to expand capacity and perform up to 796 experiments simultaneously.
- **The ability to record directly inside an incubator,** preserving physiological culture conditions during data acquisition.
- **Compatibility with both benchtop and microscope-based workflows,** providing flexibility across laboratory environments.


Together, these capabilities allow researchers to move beyond proof-of-concept studies and toward robust, high-content screening workflows that can support both discovery and development programs.


### Building a Scalable 3D Neural Screening Workflow


Oscillution has established a standardized workflow for generating large batches of human pluripotent stem cell-derived neural stem cells that differentiate into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendroglial cells. These cells are assembled into 3D neural aggregates and cultured on[96-well MEAs](https://www.multichannelsystems.com/products/microelectrode-arrays/multiwell-mea-plates) using automated liquid-handling systems to ensure consistency and scalability. A single production batch can supply hundreds of wells across multiple plates, creating an efficient platform for large-scale screening studies. Following maturation, typically between days 28 and 45, the neural aggregates are ready for compound testing and electrophysiological assessment. Analysis tools provided through the Incub8 ecosystem allow detailed characterization of compound-induced changes in neuronal activity and network behavior.


### Rapid Functional Maturation in Human 3D Neural Aggregates


The above figure shows an example of the emergence and development of spiking, network bursting, and local field potentials over 45 days in Oscillution’s 3D neural aggregates cultured on 96-well MEAs.


Spiking activity and network bursts are highlighted in blue (a), while local field potentials (LFPs; filtered <10 Hz) are shown in (d). Each well contains three recording electrodes. The mean firing rate shown in (b) provides a complementary visualization of the occurrence and development of network bursting. Typically, neuronal network bursts are preceded by accumulating spiking activity and followed by a period of neuronal inactivity, indicated by the transient absence of spiking (c). The filtered MEA recordings shown in (d) demonstrate that local field potentials are detectable during synchronous network-bursting events.


This demonstrates that electrophysiological hallmarks typically recorded from brain tissue, including network bursting and local field potentials, can also be detected in Oscillution’s human 3D neural aggregates cultured on MEAs.


Assessment of overall spiking activity and neuronal network parameters demonstrated that, while the onset of synchronous network bursting typically occurs between days 10 and 14, the 3D neural aggregates continue to mature, with the typical optimal compound-testing window occurring between days 28 and 45.


### Applying 96-Well MEAs to Drug Discovery and Development


Oscillution has also established several human *in vitro* seizure models using its human 3D neural aggregates on 96-well MEAs. These models cover a broad range of seizure mechanisms, including enhanced neuronal excitability and altered glutamatergic or GABAergic synaptic transmission. Different compounds and experimental conditions are used to modulate key targets involved in seizure generation, including voltage-gated potassium (Kv) channels, AMPA and NMDA receptors, and GABAA receptors.


The above figure shows representative data from the 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) seizure model. Clinically approved anti-seizure drugs targeting different ion channels and neurotransmitter systems effectively modulate seizure-like network activity, demonstrating the functional presence and pharmacological accessibility of key targets, including voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels and GABA(_A) receptors (a).


A key advantage of the 96-well MEA format is the ability to evaluate multiple compound concentrations in parallel while retaining sufficient capacity for vehicle and other control conditions on the same plate. This enables robust plate-level quality control, direct comparison of treatment and control conditions, and reliable concentration–response assessment.


The Incub8-Analyser allows visualization of single-electrode activity across different concentrations which provides an immediate overview of compound effects, as illustrated by the concentration-dependent suppression of seizure-like activity by perampanel, an AMPA receptor antagonist. This can subsequently be complemented by detailed quantitative analysis of electrophysiological parameters, such as the concentration-dependent reduction in network bursting relative to vehicle controls (b).


Importantly, the concentration-dependent effects of perampanel obtained using the three-electrode 96-well configuration closely reproduced those previously demonstrated with a nine-electrode MEA system \[4\]. This supports the use of the three-electrode configuration for reliable assessment of compound effects while providing the substantially increased throughput of the 96-well format.
